objectives: Describe money as an agreement between people rather than a thing with value in itself.
Name the three jobs money does and give a worked example of each one.
Explain what a bank balance and a banknote really are, and why the promise behind them has to hold.
Separate money from wealth, and a stock of money from a flow of income.
Find the costs that money carries without an invoice: tax in the price, inflation, fees, interest and the spread.
Tell a nominal figure from a real one when you read a statement or a news report.
Use plain steps to check the flow, the stock, the real value and the hidden costs of any money question.

sections.body:
Money is not a thing that has value inside it. A coin is metal, a note is paper, and both are almost worthless as material. What makes them money is an agreement between people: you give me the note, I give you what you want, and we both accept that the other side will do the same with somebody else.

The agreement works because everybody expects it. When you hand over a note in a shop, you are not trusting the note. You are trusting the shop to accept it, and the shop is trusting you to accept the change. That mutual expectation is the whole of it.

The test is simple: if nobody else would take it from you, it is not money, however much it cost to make. This is why the same piece of paper can be worth a lot in one place and nothing in another. The number of people who will accept it is the value of it.

The money of a country is called its **currency**. The currency is not the metal or the paper. It is the shared habit of using those notes and coins, and the promise behind them.
examples: The note in my wallet is paper. I hand it over because the shop will take it.
Money works here because everybody else accepts it.
The currency of this country is the dollar, and the shop takes dollars only.
sections.heading: What money is: an agreement between people

terms.example: The shop takes only the local currency.
terms.gloss: The money of a country: its notes, its coins, and the rules that govern them.

sections.body:
Money does three jobs, and each one answers a different question. The **first job is to be a medium of exchange**: money is used to pay for something instead of trading one good for another. Without money, every trade has to find somebody who wants exactly what you have. You want a ride; the driver wants rice, not your spare part. Money breaks that deadlock. The everyday version is the bus ticket: you put 2 $ in the box, and the driver gives you the ride.

The **second job is to be a unit of account**: money is the common measure of what things cost. A coffee costs 3 $, a bus ticket costs 2 $, a monthly phone bill costs 40 $. Because every price is written in the same money, you can compare two prices at a glance and know which one costs more. Without a common measure, you would have to carry the other goods around to compare them.

The **third job is to be a store of value**: money keeps its value over time, so a payment can be made today for something received later. Money lets the two sides of a deal be separated in time. A worker is paid at the end of the month for work done during the month; a shop takes the money now for goods it will deliver next month. The everyday version is the note you keep in a drawer and spend in a week, or the balance you leave in an account.

A thing can do one of these jobs well and the others badly. A bus pass is a fine medium of exchange for the ride and a poor store of value, because it expires and cannot be turned back into money. A gold coin keeps value over years and is a clumsy medium of exchange, because nobody accepts it at the bus stop. Money does all three at once, and that is why it stays in use.
examples: The fare is a medium of exchange: the money buys the ride.
At 3 $ the coffee and 2 $ the ticket, the unit of account lets me compare them.
The money in the account is a store of value for the bill that arrives next month.
sections.heading: The three jobs money does

terms.example: The bus ticket is a medium of exchange: the fare buys the ride.
terms.gloss: The job money does when it is used to pay for something instead of trading goods for goods.

terms.example: At 3 $ the coffee and 2 $ the ticket, the unit of account makes the two prices comparable.
terms.gloss: The job money does when it is the common measure of what things cost.

terms.example: The balance in the account is a store of value for the bill that arrives next month.
terms.gloss: The job money does when it keeps its value over time, so a payment can be made today for something received later.

sections.body:
Most money today is not metal. In most countries, most of the money people hold is a number in a bank account, not a note in a wallet. A **bank balance is a record**: a line in the bank's books that says the bank owes you that amount. The money does not sit in the safe and wait for you. The balance is the evidence of a promise the bank has made to you. If the bank fails, that record is worth exactly what the promise is worth.

A **banknote is a promise** as well. It is a claim on the bank that issued it, and the issuer has to redeem it on demand. The paper and the ink carry none of this. The promise is what the note stands for.

That promise has two supports. The first is **law**: the note is legal tender, the issuer is required to redeem it, and the **central bank** stands behind it. The central bank is the public body with the right to issue the currency of a country, and it sets interest rates to keep prices steady. The second support is trust: people accept the note because they expect the next person to accept it, and because they expect the issuer to pay. Law and trust are the same promise seen from two sides, one from the state and one from the people.

This is why **credit** sits at the centre of money. Credit means that somebody has been trusted to pay later. A bank deposit is credit that the bank gives to you; a banknote is credit that the issuer gives to the holder. Money works because most of it is a promise that everybody expects to be kept, and the ones who keep it are the banks and the state. One more word belongs here: **seigniorage** is the gain a state earns from issuing money. A note costs far less to make than the goods it buys, and the difference is a gain for the state.
examples: The balance is a record of a promise, not the money itself.
A banknote is a claim on the issuer, and the issuer has to pay it.
The central bank issues the notes and stands behind them.
sections.heading: Money is mostly credit: a record and a promise

terms.example: The deposit is credit: the bank owes you the balance until you spend it.
terms.gloss: A promise to pay later that somebody has been trusted to keep.

terms.example: The central bank raises its interest rate when prices rise too fast.
terms.gloss: The public body with the right to issue the currency of a country.

terms.example: The state's gain from a new note is seigniorage, because the note costs less to make than it buys.
terms.gloss: The gain a state earns from issuing money.

sections.body:
Three things are often confused with money. Keeping them apart makes the rest of the subject easier.

**Money is not wealth.** Wealth is the value of what a person owns, after what the person owes: a house, a machine, stock in a shop, the tools of a trade. Money is a claim on such goods, not the goods themselves. If everybody converted all their money into goods at the same moment, there would not be enough goods to buy, and the prices would rise. The money would not have made anybody richer.

**Money is not income.** Income is a **flow**: an amount that arrives over a period, such as a salary of 2 000 $ a month. The balance on an account is a **stock**: an amount at one moment. The two answer different questions. The flow tells you how fast money comes in; the stock tells you how much you have now. A person can have a good flow and no stock left at the end of the month, or a large stock and no flow, and the second situation ends when the stock runs out.

**Money is not the value of the thing it buys.** A 100 $ note is not a 100 $ coffee. It is a claim that the issuer owes you, and that claim passes from hand to hand. When you buy a 3 $ coffee with a 100 $ note, you take away something the seller values at 3 $ and hand over a claim worth 100 $. The number on the note and the value of the good are two different numbers. This is where **nominal** and **real** enter. A **nominal** figure is the number on the ticket: 100 $, 3 $, 2 000 $ a month. A **real** figure is what that number buys. When prices rise, the nominal number can stay the same while the real value falls.
examples: A full drawer of notes is not a fortune; it is a claim on the goods of the whole economy.
The salary is the flow; the balance on the account is the stock.
That is the nominal figure. What is the real value?
sections.heading: What money is not: wealth, income and value

terms.example: The van and the tools are wealth; the loan on the van is not.
terms.gloss: The value of what a person owns, after what the person owes.

terms.example: The stock is 800 $ today, whatever the monthly flow was.
terms.gloss: An amount measured at one moment, such as the balance on an account today.

terms.example: A flow of 2 000 $ a month leaves a stock of 300 $ after the bills.
terms.gloss: An amount measured over a period, such as the salary received in one month.

terms.example: The nominal salary is 2 000 $, which is not the same as what it buys.
terms.gloss: A figure measured in the money as printed, with no adjustment for prices.

terms.example: With prices rising, the real value of the 2 000 $ falls while the ticket still says 2 000 $.
terms.gloss: A figure adjusted for prices, so it says what the money can actually buy.

sections.body:
Most of the costs of money are not written on the receipt. The receipt shows the price. It does not show the tax that is already inside the price, the gap between the price the shop pays and the price the shop charges, the fee the card company takes, or the interest the bank charges on what you owe.

These costs are not secret, but they are easy to miss, because each one is small and each one sits somewhere else. A **tax in the price** is already counted inside the number you read. A **fee** is a fixed charge for a service, such as a card payment or a bank transfer. **Interest** is the price of borrowing money, taken as a percentage of what you still owe, and **debt** is what you owe, the base on which that interest is charged. A **spread** is the difference between the price a shop buys at and the price it sells at.

The way to see them is simple: for every payment you make, ask what else is inside it. The price is the start of the question, not the end of it.
examples: That is a price, not a fee.
The tax is already inside the price, so the receipt does not show it.
The interest is charged on the debt, not on the invoice.
sections.heading: The costs that never reach the invoice

rows: A tax that is already counted inside the price you read.
Compare the price before tax with the price on the receipt: a ticket at 10 $ plus 10 % tax is 11 $, and the receipt shows only 11 $.
The general rise of prices, which takes a share of every payment you make.
Compare the price of one item you buy regularly with the price you paid for it a year ago.
The spread the shop keeps between the price it buys at and the price it sells at.
Compare the shop price with the producer's price. The gap between them is already inside what you paid.
A fee charged by the card company for a payment or for the month.
Read the schedule of charges: it lists the fee for each payment and the fee for the year.
Interest: the price of borrowing, charged as a percentage of the debt.
Find the rate and the period on the contract, and work out what one month of interest costs on the amount you still owe.
A bank fee for keeping the account or for a service such as a transfer.
Read the fee schedule of the account: it lists what each service costs and when it is charged.

terms.example: The ticket at 11 $ includes 1 $ of tax in the price, and the receipt does not show it separately.
terms.gloss: A tax that is already counted inside the price you read.

terms.example: The spread between the producer's price and the shelf price is already inside what you pay.
terms.gloss: The difference between the price a shop buys at and the price it sells at.

terms.example: The bank fee for the transfer is 2 $ every time, whatever the amount transferred.
terms.gloss: A fixed charge for a service, such as a card payment or a bank transfer.

terms.example: At 2 % a year on a debt of 1 000 $, the interest for the year is 20 $.
terms.gloss: The price of borrowing money, charged as a percentage of what you still owe.

terms.example: The debt is 1 000 $, and the interest is charged on the part that is still left.
terms.gloss: What you owe to somebody, and the amount the interest is charged on.

sections.body:
Once money is understood as a promise, a tool and a record, the everyday questions become easier to answer. The six steps below work on any situation: a salary, a bill, a loan, a purchase.

The order matters. The flow comes first, because it tells you the direction of the movement. The stock comes second, because it tells you where you stand. The real value comes third, because a number on its own says nothing about what it buys. The hidden costs come fourth, because they are the part of the price nobody showed you. The promises come fifth, because money you cannot explain is money you cannot check. The last step is the summary in one sentence, because a definition you cannot say out loud is not yet clear to you.
examples: First the flow, then the stock, then the real value.
The cash flow is positive, and the stock is still low.
Before I sign, I want to know who has to pay me.
sections.heading: How to think about money in plain words
steps: Name the flow: write down what comes in and what goes out over one month, and put them in two columns.
Separate the stock from the flow: note the balance on the account today, and keep it apart from the money that arrived during the month.
Check the real value: take the figure you have and ask what it buys today, not what it buys on the paper.
Look for the hidden costs: read the price, the tax inside it, the fees, and the interest on what you owe.
Name the promises: ask who issued the money, who owes it, and what the law says about it.
Say it in one sentence: in plain words, what this money is, and who has to pay you.

terms.example: Cash flow is positive, but the stock is not there.
terms.gloss: The money that comes in over a period minus the money that goes out over it.

sections.body:
This article explains what money is. It explains the three jobs money does, what a bank balance and a banknote really are, what money is not, and where the hidden costs sit. It does not tell you what to buy, what to save, or where to put your money, and it does not compare one product with another.

The reason is simple. Those decisions depend on your own situation, on the prices where you live, and on rules that change from one year to the next. A general article can give you the words for the question; only you can answer the question. When a product is offered to you, read the price, read the fees, and use the questions in this article first.
examples: This article explains the idea, it does not recommend a product.
Read the price and the fees, and then decide for yourself.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
These are the sentences that make a conversation about money exact. Most disagreements about money are disagreements about a stock and a flow, or about a price and a fee, and naming the difference settles half of them.

Use the real value when the point is what something buys. Use the nominal value when the point is the number on the ticket. Say which one you are using, every time.
examples: Cash flow is positive, but the stock is not there.
That is a price, not a fee.
The balance is a record of a promise, not the money itself.
This is the nominal figure; tell me the real one.
The tax is already inside the price.
A 100 $ note is a claim, not 100 $ of coffee.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use about money

item.summary: Money is an agreement, not a thing with value in itself. After reading this you can name the three jobs money does, say what a bank balance and a banknote really are, separate a stock of money from a flow of income, find the costs that never reach the invoice, and tell a nominal figure from a real one.
item.title: What Money Is: A Promise, a Tool and a Record
